newsitem.title: GERMANY: E.German border guards guilty of Cold War killings.
newsitem.headline: E.German border guards guilty of Cold War killings.

text.p: Two former East German border guards were convicted of manslaughter on Wednesday for shooting to death a 34-year-old East German man who was trying to escape across the German-German border to the West in 1982.

A state court in the eastern town of Muehlhausen found the two border guards guilty of the Cold War killings even though they said they were following orders from their superiors. The court said they had violated the "higher law of human rights".
The two guards were sentenced to three years' probation.

The conviction was the first since the German supreme court last week ruled that East German leaders could be jailed for border killings and claims from defendants that they were only following orders was an unsufficient justification.
Borrowing the high court's language, the state court in Muehlhausen in the eastern state of Thuringen said the shoot to kill orders could not justify the slaying of the refugee.

"With their shots they were violating a higher law of human rights," the court said. "There can be no justification for the defendants' actions. The violation of human rights on the German-German border represents a severe abuse of generally accepted human rights."
German courts have previously convicted 29 lower-ranking border guards for killings but gave most of them suspended sentences because they were young recruits following orders.

Six former East German generals in charge of border security were sentenced in a landmark case in September to prison terms of between three to six years for instructing guards on how to shoot and lay mines to stop refugees.
Following the high court ruling last week, they will soon begin serving prison terms.

The extreme secrecy surrounding East Germany's fortified borders has made it impossible to know how many people were shot dead or killed by landmines as they tried to flee west from the 1950s to the fall of the Wall on November 9, 1989.
The August 13 Society, named after the day the Berlin Wall was built in 1961, said its research had uncovered at least 807 deaths along the Wall.
